                    ### Question
                    A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because she is concerned he is having another stroke. The patient says he woke up with right-sided facial weakness and drooping. Past medical history is significant for a recent case of shingles treated with acyclovir, and a stroke, diagnosed 10 years ago, from which he recovered with no residual functional deficits. On physical examination, there is weakness and drooping of the entire right side of the face. Sensation is intact. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following additional findings would also most likely be seen in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Decreased salivation
opb. Partial hearing loss
opc. Complete loss of taste to the tongue
opd. Wrinkled forehead
ope. Expressive aphasia

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's right-sided facial weakness and drooping of the entire right side of the face, with intact sensation, suggest a peripheral facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, such as Bell's palsy, rather than a central stroke. In peripheral facial nerve palsy, additional findings can include decreased salivation and partial hearing loss due to the involvement of the chorda tympani and the nerve to the stapedius, respectively. Complete loss of taste to the tongue is unlikely as the chorda tympani typically affects taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not complete loss. A wrinkled forehead would not be expected in peripheral facial nerve palsy, as the entire side of the face is affected, unlike in central lesions where the forehead is spared. Expressive aphasia is related to central brain lesions affecting language centers, not peripheral facial nerve issues. Therefore, decreased salivation and partial hearing loss are the most likely additional findings in this patient, aligning with the consensus on peripheral facial nerve involvement.
